abstract: Class IIa histone deacetylases (HDACs) have minimal HDAC activity but may function as multiprotein interaction hubs. Here, we demonstrated the expression of histone deacetylase 7 (HDAC7), a class IIa HDAC family member, in glioblastoma tumor tissue from 84 patients, patient-derived glioma stem cells from six patients, and pediatric diffuse pontine glioma cells from three patients. HDAC7 binds to histone H3.3 and interacts with H3.3 and HIRA on chromatin. Targeted downregulation of HDAC7 expression with a subtype-specific siRNA inhibits the interaction of H3.3 with HIRA, increasing the association of H3.3 with DAXX and histone lysine trimethylation at lysine 9 (H3K9me3), leading to H3.3 deposition on H3K9me3 + /4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole + heterochromatin nuclear foci. HDAC7 inhibition triggers H3K9me3 + heterochromatin spreading, increased H3K9me3 binding in the cancer genome, and significant alterations in gene expression. Using single-molecule DNA fiber analysis, we showed that HDAC7 inhibition resulted in a significant increase in replication fork speed without affecting fork symmetry, leading to replication stress, phosphorylation of RPA2, and reduced 5-ethynyl-2′-deoxyuridine incorporation. HDAC7 depletion also reduces BRCA2 expression and increases cancer cell sensitivity to DNA-damaging agents. These findings reveal the role of HDAC7 in the euchromatic H3.3 chaperone network and the impact of HDAC7 depletion on chromatin dynamics, epigenetic restriction, and DNA damage in cancer cells.
methods:
Experimental procedures
Sex as a biological variable
In our study, glioblastoma stem cells were isolated from tissues collected from both male and female patients. Similar findings were reported in both cases.
Primary glioblastoma stem cell isolation and culture
The Institutional Review Board of Rhode Island Hospital approved the collection of patient-derived glioblastoma tissues. All collections were performed with written informed consent from patients in a completely deidentified manner, and the studies were performed in accordance with the recognized ethical guidelines (Belmont Report). Primary GSC spheres were cultured from human glioma samples, as previously described (
52
). The GSCs used in this study were authenticated by the American Type Culture Collection using short tandem repeat analysis. GSCs used were between passages 5 and 30 and cultured either as spheres or attached on fibronectin-coated plates (10 mg/ml, MilliporeSigma) in 1X neurobasal medium, B27 serum-free supplement, minus vitamin A, 100X Glutamax (Fisher Scientific), 1 mg/ml heparin (STEMCELL Technologies), 20 ng/ml epidermal growth factor (Peprotech), and 20 ng/ml basic fibroblast growth factor (FGF; Peprotech). All GSC cultures were routinely tested for Mycoplasma contamination using a MycoSensor qPCR assay (Agilent).
DIPG cells and primary human astrocytes
Primary DIPG cells were a kind gift from Dr Monje and isolated from pediatric patients with DIPG at the Stanford University. The cells were cultured in serum-free media containing basic FGF, epidermal growth factor, and platelet-derived growth factor.
Primary human astrocytes were purchased from ScienCell (catalog no.: 1800) and maintained per the manufacturer’s instructions.
Analysis of publicly available cancer datasets
For survival analysis, we used the Cancer Genome Atlas patient cohort. Patients were assigned to high- or low-risk groups based on HDAC7 expression levels. The datasets were downloaded from GlioVis and visualized using Kaplan–Meier Plotter (
53
), GlioVis (
54
) web tools, and the R Bioconductor package.
Nanostring PanCancer progression analysis
We collected RNA from 84 formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded samples from glioblastoma patients and performed gene expression analysis using the Nanostring PanCancer progression panel, which comprises vital components of pathways involved in the complex interplay between the tumor and its microenvironment. Overall survival was estimated by the Kaplan–Meier method using GraphPad Prism (GraphPad Software, Inc). Pathway enrichment and Gene Ontology enrichment analyses were performed on differentially expressed genes using the R package DESeq (
55
).
siRNA transfection
GSCs were grown on fibronectin/Hank’s balanced salt solution–treated culture plates in antibiotic-free media supplemented with Neurobasal-A, B-27-A, Glutamax, growth factors (epidermal growth factor and FGF), and heparin, and GSCs were incubated at 37 °C with 5% CO
2

The tumor sphere formation assay was performed as previously described (

RNA sequencing
Next-generation RNA-Seq was performed using the Illumina HiSeq2500 system (Azenta). Sequence reads were aligned with the human genome using

Mass spectrometry for histone modifications (Mod-Spec)
Five million GSCs were harvested, washed twice with PBS, and snap-frozen. Successful knockdown of HDAC7 was confirmed by Western blotting, and the samples were sent to the Active Motif to perform Mod-Spec per in-house protocol. The entire MS process was repeated three times for each sample. The data were quantified using Skyline (MacCoss Lab, Univeristy of Washington) (
57
) and presented as the percentage of each modification within the total pool of tryptic peptides.
Rapid immunoprecipitation mass spectrometry of endogenous protein
Two biological replicates of GSCs (5 × 10
8
cells per replicate) were fixed for 8 min with a formaldehyde solution of 11% methanol-free formaldehyde, 0.1 M NaCl (Invitrogen), 1 mM EDTA, pH 8 (Invitrogen), and 50 mM Hepes, pH 7.9 (Fisher BioReagents). Fixation was stopped using a 2.5 M glycine solution in water (Sigma). Fixed cells were washed with chilled PBS-Igepal (0.5% Igepal CA-630 in PBS) and PMSF (Active Motif). The washed cells were centrifuged, pelleted, snap-frozen on dry ice, and sent to Active Motif for RIME service (
58
). PEAKS Studio was used for visualization and analysis, and the “Decoy Fused Method” was applied to calculate FDR, where the default cutoff was set to −10log
P
> 20 to ensure high-quality peptide spectrum matches and increase confidence in the obtained protein list.
Co-IP followed by Western blot
After the respective courses of treatment, GSCs (10 million cells/Co-IP) were collected and prepared for nuclear extraction and purification using a nuclear extraction kit (Active Motif). Nuclear extracts were treated with an enzymatic shearing cocktail for DNA digestion to release undissociated protein complexes, including histone proteins and DNA-binding proteins, from the DNA. Extracted and purified nuclear lysates (500 μg) were used per IP after preclearing with normal IgG (the same concentration as the respective IP antibody) for 1 h on a rotator at 4 °C. Precleared nuclear lysates were then combined with 25 μl of Protein G beads and incubated for 1 h on a rotator at 4 °C to remove any IgG nonspecific binding. After separating the magnetic beads on a magnetic stand, the collected nuclear supernatant was then combined with IP antibodies of either 1 μg HDAC7 (Cell Signaling) or 4 μg H3.3 (Abcam) and incubated for 4 h on a rotator at 4 °C. The immunoprecipitated samples were then combined with 25 μl of Protein G beads and incubated for 1 h on a rotator at 4 °C. After separating the magnetic beads on a magnetic stand, the immunoprecipitated samples (now bound to the beads) were washed four times with co-IP wash buffer (Active Motif). The washed immunoprecipitated samples bound to beads were then resuspended in 20 μl of 2X Reducing Loading Buffer (130 mM Tris [pH 6.8], 4% SDS, 0.02% bromophenol blue, 20% glycerol, and 100 mM DTT) and boiled at 95 °C for 5 min. The magnetic beads were separated from the desaturated samples using a magnetic stand. All extraction and IP steps were performed in buffers supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitors to limit further protein modifications (expression, proteolysis, dephosphorylation, etc.). Immunoprecipitated samples were analyzed by Western blotting.
Histone lysate extraction and purification
Histone acid precipitation was used to extract pure crude histones from GSCs following transfection. After treatment, GSCs were detached using StemPro Accutase (Gibco), and spun-down pellets were collected. The pellets were then resuspended in an appropriate volume of ice-cold histone extraction buffer (Active Motif) and incubated overnight at 4 °C on a rotator. The next day, the cell suspensions were centrifuged to collect the core histone extracts. Acid extractions were pH-measured and neutralized with the required volume of 5X neutralization buffer until complete neutralization was achieved. Core histones were purified by column elution, and the purified histone lysates were stored at −80 °C for downstream experiments.
H3K9Me3 ELISA
Purified core histone extracts prepared as described previously were quantified for H3K9me3 following ELISA protocols from the active motif (catalog no.: 53109). Absorbance at 450 nm with a reference wavelength of 655 nm was measured on a Promega GloMax Plate Reader. Absorbance was normalized after subtracting the blank wells. Quantification of methyl Lys9 from histone H3 in the samples was performed using a standard curve plotted in GraphPad Prism.
Electron microscopy
Treated GSCs were harvested, and pellets were resuspended in 5 ml volume of fixative master mix of paraformaldehyde–glutaraldehyde solution, Karnovsky's fixative (Electron Microscopy Sciences). Fixative solution was prepared with 16% paraformaldehyde solution, 5% glutaraldehyde EM grade, and 0.2 M sodium phosphate buffer. Fixed samples were outsourced to the Charles River Laboratories for EM imaging services (Frederick PAI Project No.: 20354508). Each sample was examined using a transmission electron microscope, and up to 10 representative digital images per sample were captured using an AMT camera.
Immunofluorescence
Primary glioblastoma stem cells were seeded in complete media without heparin on cell culture–treated chamber slides (Ibidi) overnight and transfected after 24 h with 2x lipid (Mirus Bio) and either 25 nM control (Horizon) or HDAC7 (Horizon) siRNA. Immunofluorescence staining was performed 48 h post-transfection.
For H3.3, cells were fixed/permeabilized with 100% ice-cold methanol for 5 min and incubated in blocking buffer (1% bovine serum albumin [BSA], 10% donkey serum, 22.52 mg/ml glycine in PBS + 0.1% Tween-20 for 1 h at room temperature. The primary antibody (Abcam) was applied at 1:1000 dilution in primary antibody buffer (1% BSA in PBS + 0.1% Tween-20) overnight at 4 °C. Cells were washed with Dulbecco’s PBS (DPBS), incubated with secondary antibody (Jackson) in 1:100 dilution in DPBS for 1 h, and mounted with DAPI (Vector Labs).
For H3k9me3, cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (methanol free) for 10 min, permeabilized with 0.1% Triton in DPBS for 5 min. Blocking, primary antibody (Active Motif), secondary antibody, and mounting were applied as described previously.
Images were taken using a Zeiss Axiovert Inverted Microscope with Apotome II.
H3K9me3 ChIP-Seq
GSCs were seeded and transfected with siRNA against HDAC7 for 48 h and then processed for ChIP-Seq using the standard Active Motif ChIP-IT ChIP-Seq protocol. Cells reached a confluency of 80% post-transfection and were then fixed in 1% formaldehyde. Following fixation, the samples were sonicated, and sheared chromatin was immunoprecipitated using a ChIP-validated H3K9me3 antibody (Active Motif). The ChIP DNA was then reverse crosslinked, and DNA was collected for library preparation and sequencing.
ChIP-Seq analysis
Following library preparation, the 75-nt single-end (SE75) sequence reads generated by Illumina sequencing were mapped to the genome using the Burrows–Wheeler Aligner algorithm with default settings and filtered out reads with more than two mismatches and with no unique alignment. The reads were extended to a length of 200 bp using Active Motif software and subsequently divided into bins and stored as a bigwig file. Following read alignment and density identification, SICER was used for peak calling at the default settings (FDR 1e-10 with a gap parameter of 600 bp). Peak filtering was performed by removing the false ChIP-Seq peaks from the ENCODE blacklist. Spike-in chromatin analysis was performed, and the number of test tags was adjusted for normalization. For annotation, peaks were associated with genes if found within the 10 kb upstream/downstream limit.
H3.3 CUT&Tag
Samples were transfected with siHDAC7 or siControl as described previously (n = 2 per condition). To ensure sufficient cells for the protocol, we combined two 60 mm dishes per sample. Forty-eight hours after transfection, cells were collected following a protocol provided by Active Motif. Sample viability was measured before freezing overnight in 50% fetal bovine serum, 40% complete medium, and 10% dimethyl sulfoxide. CUT&Tag was performed by Active Motif as a service using an H3.3-validated antibody.
Proximity ligation assay
Cells were seeded at a density of 2.5 × 10
4
cells on fibronectin-coated 10 mm German Glass coverslips placed in 4-well plates and cultured for 24 h. The cells were washed once with PBS, fixed in methanol for 5 min at room temperature, and then blocked for an hour using Duolink Blocking Solution. All subsequent washes were 4 ml at room temperature, and the coverslips were transferred to 6-well plates. All reactions and incubations occurred on parafilm taped inside a humidity chamber. HDAC7 antibody was added at a 1:100 dilution into Duolink Antibody Diluent, 50 μl was placed on each coverslip, and incubated overnight at 4 °C. The coverslips were washed three times in 4 ml of 1× wash buffer A for 5 min each. The anti-rabbit PLUS probe was diluted 1:5 in the Duolink Antibody Diluent, and 40 μl was applied to each coverslip and incubated for 1 h at 37 °C. The coverslips were washed three times with 1× wash buffer A for 5 min. The conjugated H3.3-MINUS antibody (created with the Duolink Probemaker MINUS) was diluted at 1:300 in PLA probe diluent, and 50 μl was added to each coverslip and incubated overnight at 4 °C. The coverslips were washed three times with 1× wash buffer A for 5 min. The 5× Duolink ligation buffer was diluted 1:5 in high-purity water, and the ligase was added at a 1:40 dilution immediately before adding 40 μl of the mix to the coverslips. The cells were then incubated for 30 min at 37 °C. The coverslips were washed three times with 1× wash buffer A for 5 min. The 5× Duolink amplification buffer was diluted 1:5 in high-purity water, and the polymerase was added in a 1:80 dilution immediately before applying 40 μl of the amplification solution to the coverslips and incubated for 100 min at 37 °C. The amplification buffer was light sensitive and protected from light throughout as well as for all subsequent steps. The slides were washed two times in 1× wash buffer B for 10 min, then one time in 0.01× wash buffer B for 1 min. Two coverslips were mounted onto each slide using the Vectashield Mounting Medium with DAPI. They were left to dry for at least 1 h and imaged using the 83× objective on a Zeiss Axio Imager with the ApoTome 2.0. The slides were stored at −20 °C. Negative controls with either the conjugated H3.3-MINUS antibody or the HDAC7 antibody were excluded.
DNA fiber assay
GSCs were transfected with siControl or siHDAC7 as described above. DNA fiber assays were performed according to previously published protocols (
59
). Quantification of fibers from three images obtained from two independent experiments was performed using a semiautomated technique available in the DNA Stranding software package (
60
). In each group, individual fibers were segmented automatically using the software’s prespecified input parameters, and the 20-min pulse labeling of chlorodeoxyuridine and iododeoxyuridine was selected according to the DNA fiber assay protocol. After automatic segmentation, a manual review of individual fiber labels was conducted to remove erroneously selected fiber segmentations and correct apparent mistakes, in line with previously published methods. A total of 291 fibers from cells transfected with siControl and 167 fibers from cells transfected with siHDAC7 were identified and quantified in the final analysis. Quantitative comparison of replication fork speed and chlorodeoxyuridine and iododeoxyuridine ratio metrics was performed using GraphPad Prism.
Cell cycle analysis using flow cytometry
About 250,000 cells were seeded on 6-well plates, and individual wells were treated with siHDAC7 or siCTRL (50 nM final concentration) using lipid transfection as described previously. Separate samples were collected for Western blotting confirmation of siHDAC7 knockdown. For fluorescence-activated cell sorting experiments, pairs of wells treated with identical conditions were combined to yield six total samples, three from each condition. For EdU, the Click-iT Plus EdU Alexa Fluor 647 Flow Cytometry Assay Kit was used (Invitrogen; catalog no.:
C10634
), and for propidium iodide (PI), we used FxCycle PI/RNase Staining Solution (Life Technologies; catalog no.:
F10797
). EdU (10 μM) was added to each well, and cells were incubated for 1 to 2 h. Cells were then lifted from plates using StemPro Accutase (ThermoFisher; catalog no.: A1110501), collected using PBS, spun at 230
g
for 5 min, washed with 2 ml 1% BSA in PBS, spun at 230
g
for 5 min again, and then fixed using Click-iT Fixative according to the kit instructions. Samples were then washed once again with 1% BSA in PBS, spun again at 230
g
for 5 min, and then permeabilized and incubated with 250 μl FxCycle PI/RNase Staining Solution, otherwise according to kit instructions. A Cytek Aurora system was used for flow cytometry. Unstained control samples of the same cells treated with the same siRNAs were also used for normalization.

First, CSK buffer was prepared with a final pH = 6.8 and consisting of the following components, in water: 10 mM Pipes, 100 mM NaCl, 300 mM sucrose, 3 mM MgCl
2

After plating GSCs on 6-well clear-bottomed plates in transfection media (350,000/well), the cells were transfected after 24 h with siCTRL or siHDAC7. The cell lysates were collected after 48 h. Additional siHDAC7-transfected cells were treated with etoposide (50 μM) for 30 and 120 min after treatment. For collection of lysates, cells from individual wells were detached from the plate using StemPro Accutase, spun for 5 min at 230
g
to pellet, and the pellet was resuspended in 500 μl of CSK buffer on ice for 30 min and vortexed every 5 to 10 min. The samples were then centrifuged at 4 °C for 10 min at 10,000

The pellet was then resuspended in 100 μl Laemmli buffer (99 μl 1% SDS plus 1 μl phosphatase inhibitor cocktail). The samples were then sonicated and heated to 95 °C to denature the proteins in preparation for Western blotting.

body:
Epigenetic mechanisms have emerged as key players in cancer development. Alterations in chromatin mediate cell reprogramming and oncogenesis, whereas epigenetic changes triggered by the tumor microenvironment regulate cancer cell phenotypic transitions and tumor architecture (
1
,
2
). Chromatin exists in two higher-order states: euchromatin refers to loosely packed chromatin that is easily accessible to transcriptional regulators and RNA polymerase, whereas heterochromatin is densely packed and not accessible (
3
,
4
). Alteration of the state of chromatin affects global gene expression by making genes either more or less accessible for transcription. Interconversion between these two chromatin states occurs through the function of several regulators that affect the levels of DNA methylation or post-translational modifications of histones (acetylation, methylation, phosphorylation, sumoylation, etc.). This dynamic regulatory system is commonly referred to as epigenetic control of gene transcription (
5
).
Histone deacetylases (HDACs) remove acetyl groups from histone molecules, thereby regulating the post-translational modification of histone marks. Expression of HDACs is elevated in several tumors, resulting in the transcriptional activation of oncogenes, increased transcriptional rates, and chromosomal translocations (
4
,
6
,
7
). HDACs can be divided into class I (HDAC1, 2, 3, and 8), class II (HDAC4, 5, 6, 7, 9, and 10), and class IV (HDAC11), based on sequence similarity. Class II HDACs are further divided into class IIa (HDAC4, 5, 7, and 9) and class IIb (HDAC6 and 10) according to their domain compositions. However, class IIa HDACs lack measurable enzymatic activity, and their deacetylase activity toward acetylated histones is minimal (
5
). Compared with class I HDACs, class IIa HDACs exhibit a prolonged N-terminal region that harbors a nuclear localization signal and a nuclear export signal and are found both in the nucleus and cytoplasm (
5
). The presence of this unique N-terminal region suggests that class IIa HDACs may participate in multiprotein complexes to exert their biological functions. In human malignancies, class I and II HDACs are oncoproteins that regulate gene expression to promote tumorigenesis and cancer development (
5
,
6
,
7
). Specifically, HDAC7 has been implicated in the pathogenesis of colorectal (
8
,
9
), pancreatic (
10
,
11
), liver (
12
), gastric (
13
), lung (
14
), breast (
15
), and brain cancers (
16
,
17
).
Canonical histone proteins are incorporated into chromatin in a DNA replication–dependent manner, whereas histone H3.3 is incorporated in a DNA replication–independent manner (
18
,
19
,
20
). In
Drosophila melanogaster
and
Arabidopsis thaliana
, H3.3 is enriched in replication origins (
21
,
22
,
23
,
24
,
25
,
26
), whereas in human cells, it is associated with early replication and recruited at sites of DNA repair (
26
,
27
,
28
). Although H3.3 is mainly associated with euchromatin and regulation of active transcription (
20
,
29
), it has recently been shown to be associated with heterochromatin on telomeres, pericentric heterochromatin, and heterochromatin marks on gene regulatory regions (
29
,
30
). The association of H3.3 with euchromatin or heterochromatin is largely dependent on a group of proteins with chaperone activity that interact with H3.3 and deposit it on chromatin regions. Euchromatin deposition is regulated by a HIRA–UBN1–CABIN1 chaperone complex, whereas heterochromatin deposition of H3.3 depends on its interaction with DAXX–ATRX (
31
,
32
). The balance between HIRA–UBN1–CABIN1 and DAXX–ATRX deposition of H3.3 on euchromatin or heterochromatin, respectively, may represent a crucial node in histone landscape reprogramming that enables complex cell fate decisions during tumorigenesis. The involvement of HDACs in these histone chaperone complexes has only been suggested for the MIER1 complex but not for individual HDACs (
33
), and the participation of class IIa HDACs in the regulation of the histone H3.3 chromatin landscape has not been reported to date.
Here, we showed high expression of HDAC7 in glioblastoma tumor tissue from 84 patients, patient-derived glioma stem cells (GSCs) from six patients, and in pediatric diffuse pontine glioma (DIPG) cells from three patients. HDAC7 shows minimal HDAC activity but forms protein–protein interactions (PPIs) with histone H3.3 on chromatin. Specific inhibition of HDAC7 expression with an
in vivo
stable siRNA results in an increase in the heterochromatin mark histone lysine trimethylation at lysine 9 (H3K9me3) and heterochromatin spreading in cancer cells. Following HDAC7 inhibition, the interaction of H3.3 with HIRA was reduced, the association of H3.3 with DAXX and H3K9me3 was increased, and H3.3 was deposited on H3K9me3
+
/4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI)
+
heterochromatin nuclear foci. This results in increased spreading of H3K9me3 on the cancer genome and significant alterations in cancer cell gene expression. Inhibition of HDAC7 results in an increase in DNA replication fork speed without affecting symmetry, resulting in replication stress and a reduction in 5-ethynyl-2′-deoxyuridine (EdU) incorporation. Finally, knockdown of HDAC7 expression induced significant sensitization of cancer cells to DNA-damaging agents.
Results
HDAC7 is highly expressed in glioblastoma tumors and correlates with decreased patient survival
We compared the expression of all class IIa HDACs in glioblastoma using data from The Cancer Genome Atlas. HDAC-7 was the only class IIa HDAC with significantly higher expression in glioblastoma than in nontumor samples (
Fig. 1
A
). To show the clinical correlation of HDAC7 expression in glioblastoma, we performed survival analysis in class IIa high- and low-expressing patients. Patients were divided into two groups based on the maximally ranked statistics using the log-rank test and the Gehan–Breslow–Wilcoxon method. High HDAC7 expression patients showed a significantly lower probability of survival (
p
< 0.004) (
Fig. 1
B
), whereas the expression levels of other members of class IIa HDACs were not significantly correlated with patient survival.

Expression of HDAC7 in adult glioblastoma and pediatric DIPG cells

Class specificity of HDAC7 siRNA
To discover a target-specific siRNA for HDAC7, we designed and filtered through a BLAST similarity search and finally synthesized four individual siRNAs that target the open reading frame and 3′-untranslated region of human HDAC7. Rapid immunoprecipitation MS of endogenous proteins to identify the HDAC7 interactome within the nucleus
To investigate how HDAC7 inhibition results in an increase in heterochromatin marks, we hypothesized that HDAC7 forms multiprotein interactions within the nucleus to participate in the regulation of active transcription. We employed rapid immunoprecipitation (IP) MS of endogenous proteins (RIME) to discover the HDAC7 PPI network in the nucleus of GSCs. GSCs (n = 3) were fixed with formaldehyde to crosslink proteins and DNA in close proximity. The nuclei were then isolated, and HDAC7 IP was performed. The HDAC7 precipitated protein complex was subjected to MS, which revealed 247 proteins constituting the HDAC7 nuclear interactome. The proteins were entered into STRING for network analysis using default settings and exported to Cytoscape for network construction. Of the 247 proteins, 229 formed a highly interconnected network (

Discussion
Class IIa HDACs have limited catalytic activity in eukaryotic cells, primarily because of the substitution of tyrosine with histidine within the enzymatic pocket of these molecules (
42
). Although class IIa HDACs can bind to acetylated lysine, they do not exert deacetylase activity, and it has been proposed that they function to attract other HDAC subtypes to deacetylate substrates (
43
,
44
). Several studies have highlighted the role of class IIa HDACs in cancer, with the exact function of each member varying depending on the type of cancer (
45
). HDAC7 has been implicated in the regulation of cancer stem cell fate, specifically in breast and ovarian tumors, and overexpression of HDAC7 has been shown to increase cancer stem cell phenotype (
46
). HDAC7 binds near the transcription start sites and superenhancers of oncogenes in breast cancer stem cells and contributes to transcriptional regulation. However, the mechanism by which HDAC7 maintains H3K27Ac levels at the transcription start site and superenhancers remains unclear (
45
,
47
).
Our findings provide compelling evidence supporting the interaction between HDAC7 and histone H3.3 in glioblastoma cells. Using RIME, co-IP, and PLA, we demonstrated a specific interaction between these proteins. This adds to the growing body of literature on the complex interplay between histone molecules and their regulatory enzymes. The interaction between HDAC7 and histone H3.3 suggests a role for HDAC7 in chromatin remodeling and gene regulation.
The specific interaction with H3.3, a histone variant mainly associated with active chromatin states, underscores the importance of HDAC7 in maintaining chromatin homeostasis. Histone H3.3 is deposited into euchromatin in a DNA replication–independent manner. Specifically, H3.3 forms complexes with the histone chaperone HIRA to mediate DNA synthesis–independent nucleosome assembly (
48
). Our study revealed that HDAC7 actively participates in these euchromatin complexes by interacting with H3.3. Inhibition of HDAC7 leads to a reduction in the association of H3.3 with HIRA and an increase in its association with DAXX and H3K9me3. Consequently, the H3.3 landscape undergoes remodeling in cancer cells, resulting in the spread of heterochromatin and association of H3.3 with heterochromatin foci. Our findings revealed a novel aspect of HDAC7 biology in cancer. Notably, the observed increase in heterochromatin upon HDAC7 inhibition suggests a potential role for HDAC7 in maintaining the delicate balance between euchromatin and heterochromatin, which is often disrupted in cancer cells (
Fig. 8
F
). Although global H3K9me3 levels are elevated, our ChIP-Seq data reveal a selective redistribution of this heterochromatic mark. Fewer genomic loci gained H3K9me3, but with higher signal intensity and better-defined peaks, consistent with focal heterochromatin consolidation. In contrast, a larger number of weaker regions exhibited decreased signal, suggesting a loss of diffuse H3K9me3 from transcriptionally permissive or less-structured chromatin domains. This points to an epigenetic reprogramming process favoring the reinforcement of specific repressive hubs with high-density H3K9me3 over widespread silencing.
The heterochromatin histone mark H3K9me3 is associated with transcriptionally repressive regions of the genome and is a hallmark of constitutive heterochromatin often found in pericentromeric and telomeric regions (
49
). As cells replicate, histone marks such as H3K9me3 are diluted owing to the incorporation of new, unmodified histones. The colocalization of EdU (a marker for DNA synthesis) with H3K9me3 after inhibition of HDAC7 expression suggests that active DNA replication occurs on heterochromatin, supporting the inheritance of epigenetic states and stable gene repression.
Our data indicate that siHDAC7 treatment led to a notable disruption of cell cycle dynamics. DNA fiber analysis revealed a significant increase in replication fork speed, which may diminish the fidelity of DNA polymerases, potentially contributing to genomic instability (
41
,
50
). At the same time, the reduction in MCM 2–7 expression could explain the increased fork speed (
51
) because the cells compensate for the reduced number of licensed forks by increasing the speed of replication. Reduced MCM levels and insufficient original firing may result in fewer global replication stress signals. Notably, the reduction in BRCA2 expression could also contribute to an increase in replication speed, as shown in poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitor–treated BRCA1-deficient cells (
41
). Eventually, the increase in fork speed in conjunction with inhibition of MCM 2–7 and reduction in BRAC2 expression after depletion of HDAC7 compromises fork protection and homologous recombination, further exacerbating fork collapse. As a result, cells prematurely exit S phase and accumulate in G2 with unresolved replication intermediates, reflecting a checkpoint-leaky transition and potential for genomic instability. This DNA replication environment is particularly vulnerable to the additional stress caused by DNA-damaging agents. In fact, TMZ- and etoposide-induced lesions appear to overwhelm the repair capacity of cells, leading to significant DNA damage and increased γH2AX expression. This highlights a potential therapeutic opportunity for combining HDAC7 inhibition as a replication stress–inducing strategy with DNA-damaging agents.
This study represents a conceptual leap in understanding the role of HDAC7, transforming our perception of this enzyme from a minor player in histone modification to a central figure in chromatin dynamics and cancer cell vulnerability. The implications are vast: targeting HDAC7 could unlock new strategies to suppress oncogenic transcriptional programs, induce replication stress, and enhance the efficacy of DNA-damaging agents—all while exploring the boundaries of epigenetic reprogramming in cancer. Our findings open a window into precision medicine by targeting a previously underexplored axis of chromatin regulation, promising transformative impact across oncology and beyond.
Experimental procedures
Sex as a biological variable
In our study, glioblastoma stem cells were isolated from tissues collected from both male and female patients. Similar findings were reported in both cases.
Primary glioblastoma stem cell isolation and culture
The Institutional Review Board of Rhode Island Hospital approved the collection of patient-derived glioblastoma tissues. All collections were performed with written informed consent from patients in a completely deidentified manner, and the studies were performed in accordance with the recognized ethical guidelines (Belmont Report). Primary GSC spheres were cultured from human glioma samples, as previously described (
52
). The GSCs used in this study were authenticated by the American Type Culture Collection using short tandem repeat analysis. GSCs used were between passages 5 and 30 and cultured either as spheres or attached on fibronectin-coated plates (10 mg/ml, MilliporeSigma) in 1X neurobasal medium, B27 serum-free supplement, minus vitamin A, 100X Glutamax (Fisher Scientific), 1 mg/ml heparin (STEMCELL Technologies), 20 ng/ml epidermal growth factor (Peprotech), and 20 ng/ml basic fibroblast growth factor (FGF; Peprotech). All GSC cultures were routinely tested for Mycoplasma contamination using a MycoSensor qPCR assay (Agilent).
DIPG cells and primary human astrocytes
Primary DIPG cells were a kind gift from Dr Monje and isolated from pediatric patients with DIPG at the Stanford University. The cells were cultured in serum-free media containing basic FGF, epidermal growth factor, and platelet-derived growth factor.
Primary human astrocytes were purchased from ScienCell (catalog no.: 1800) and maintained per the manufacturer’s instructions.
Analysis of publicly available cancer datasets
For survival analysis, we used the Cancer Genome Atlas patient cohort. Patients were assigned to high- or low-risk groups based on HDAC7 expression levels. The datasets were downloaded from GlioVis and visualized using Kaplan–Meier Plotter (
53
), GlioVis (
54
) web tools, and the R Bioconductor package.
Nanostring PanCancer progression analysis
We collected RNA from 84 formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded samples from glioblastoma patients and performed gene expression analysis using the Nanostring PanCancer progression panel, which comprises vital components of pathways involved in the complex interplay between the tumor and its microenvironment. Overall survival was estimated by the Kaplan–Meier method using GraphPad Prism (GraphPad Software, Inc). Pathway enrichment and Gene Ontology enrichment analyses were performed on differentially expressed genes using the R package DESeq (
55
).

Five million GSCs were harvested, washed twice with PBS, and snap-frozen. Rapid immunoprecipitation mass spectrometry of endogenous protein
Two biological replicates of GSCs (5 × 10
8
cells per replicate) were fixed for 8 min with a formaldehyde solution of 11% methanol-free formaldehyde, 0.1 M NaCl (Invitrogen), 1 mM EDTA, pH 8 (Invitrogen), and 50 mM Hepes, pH 7.9 (Fisher BioReagents). Fixation was stopped using a 2.5 M glycine solution in water (Sigma). Fixed cells were washed with chilled PBS-Igepal (0.5% Igepal CA-630 in PBS) and PMSF (Active Motif). ). PEAKS Studio was used for visualization and analysis, and the “Decoy Fused Method” was applied to calculate FDR, where the default cutoff was set to −10log

Co-IP followed by Western blot
After the respective courses of treatment, GSCs (10 million cells/Co-IP) were collected and prepared for nuclear extraction and purification using a nuclear extraction kit (Active Motif). Nuclear extracts were treated with an enzymatic shearing cocktail for DNA digestion to release undissociated protein complexes, including histone proteins and DNA-binding proteins, from the DNA. Extracted and purified nuclear lysates (500 μg) were used per IP after preclearing with normal IgG (the same concentration as the respective IP antibody) for 1 h on a rotator at 4 °C. Precleared nuclear lysates were then combined with 25 μl of Protein G beads and incubated for 1 h on a rotator at 4 °C to remove any IgG nonspecific binding. After separating the magnetic beads on a magnetic stand, the collected nuclear supernatant was then combined with IP antibodies of either 1 μg HDAC7 (Cell Signaling) or 4 μg H3.3 (Abcam) and incubated for 4 h on a rotator at 4 °C. The immunoprecipitated samples were then combined with 25 μl of Protein G beads and incubated for 1 h on a rotator at 4 °C. After separating the magnetic beads on a magnetic stand, the immunoprecipitated samples (now bound to the beads) were washed four times with co-IP wash buffer (Active Motif). The washed immunoprecipitated samples bound to beads were then resuspended in 20 μl of 2X Reducing Loading Buffer (130 mM Tris [pH 6.8], 4% SDS, 0.02% bromophenol blue, 20% glycerol, and 100 mM DTT) and boiled at 95 °C for 5 min. The magnetic beads were separated from the desaturated samples using a magnetic stand. All extraction and IP steps were performed in buffers supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitors to limit further protein modifications (expression, proteolysis, dephosphorylation, etc.). Immunoprecipitated samples were analyzed by Western blotting.
Histone lysate extraction and purification
Histone acid precipitation was used to extract pure crude histones from GSCs following transfection. After treatment, GSCs were detached using StemPro Accutase (Gibco), and spun-down pellets were collected. The pellets were then resuspended in an appropriate volume of ice-cold histone extraction buffer (Active Motif) and incubated overnight at 4 °C on a rotator. The next day, the cell suspensions were centrifuged to collect the core histone extracts. Acid extractions were pH-measured and neutralized with the required volume of 5X neutralization buffer until complete neutralization was achieved. Core histones were purified by column elution, and the purified histone lysates were stored at −80 °C for downstream experiments.
H3K9Me3 ELISA
Purified core histone extracts prepared as described previously were quantified for H3K9me3 following ELISA protocols from the active motif (catalog no.: 53109). Absorbance at 450 nm with a reference wavelength of 655 nm was measured on a Promega GloMax Plate Reader. Absorbance was normalized after subtracting the blank wells. Quantification of methyl Lys9 from histone H3 in the samples was performed using a standard curve plotted in GraphPad Prism.
Electron microscopy
Treated GSCs were harvested, and pellets were resuspended in 5 ml volume of fixative master mix of paraformaldehyde–glutaraldehyde solution, Karnovsky's fixative (Electron Microscopy Sciences). Fixative solution was prepared with 16% paraformaldehyde solution, 5% glutaraldehyde EM grade, and 0.2 M sodium phosphate buffer. Fixed samples were outsourced to the Charles River Laboratories for EM imaging services (Frederick PAI Project No.: 20354508). Each sample was examined using a transmission electron microscope, and up to 10 representative digital images per sample were captured using an AMT camera.
Immunofluorescence
Primary glioblastoma stem cells were seeded in complete media without heparin on cell culture–treated chamber slides (Ibidi) overnight and transfected after 24 h with 2x lipid (Mirus Bio) and either 25 nM control (Horizon) or HDAC7 (Horizon) siRNA. Immunofluorescence staining was performed 48 h post-transfection.
For H3.3, cells were fixed/permeabilized with 100% ice-cold methanol for 5 min and incubated in blocking buffer (1% bovine serum albumin [BSA], 10% donkey serum, 22.52 mg/ml glycine in PBS + 0.1% Tween-20 for 1 h at room temperature. The primary antibody (Abcam) was applied at 1:1000 dilution in primary antibody buffer (1% BSA in PBS + 0.1% Tween-20) overnight at 4 °C. Cells were washed with Dulbecco’s PBS (DPBS), incubated with secondary antibody (Jackson) in 1:100 dilution in DPBS for 1 h, and mounted with DAPI (Vector Labs).
For H3k9me3, cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (methanol free) for 10 min, permeabilized with 0.1% Triton in DPBS for 5 min. Blocking, primary antibody (Active Motif), secondary antibody, and mounting were applied as described previously.
Images were taken using a Zeiss Axiovert Inverted Microscope with Apotome II.
H3K9me3 ChIP-Seq
GSCs were seeded and transfected with siRNA against HDAC7 for 48 h and then processed for ChIP-Seq using the standard Active Motif ChIP-IT ChIP-Seq protocol. Cells reached a confluency of 80% post-transfection and were then fixed in 1% formaldehyde. Following fixation, the samples were sonicated, and sheared chromatin was immunoprecipitated using a ChIP-validated H3K9me3 antibody (Active Motif). The ChIP DNA was then reverse crosslinked, and DNA was collected for library preparation and sequencing.
ChIP-Seq analysis
Following library preparation, the 75-nt single-end (SE75) sequence reads generated by Illumina sequencing were mapped to the genome using the Burrows–Wheeler Aligner algorithm with default settings and filtered out reads with more than two mismatches and with no unique alignment. The reads were extended to a length of 200 bp using Active Motif software and subsequently divided into bins and stored as a bigwig file. Following read alignment and density identification, SICER was used for peak calling at the default settings (FDR 1e-10 with a gap parameter of 600 bp). Peak filtering was performed by removing the false ChIP-Seq peaks from the ENCODE blacklist. Spike-in chromatin analysis was performed, and the number of test tags was adjusted for normalization. For annotation, peaks were associated with genes if found within the 10 kb upstream/downstream limit.
H3.3 CUT&Tag
Samples were transfected with siHDAC7 or siControl as described previously (n = 2 per condition). To ensure sufficient cells for the protocol, we combined two 60 mm dishes per sample. Forty-eight hours after transfection, cells were collected following a protocol provided by Active Motif. Sample viability was measured before freezing overnight in 50% fetal bovine serum, 40% complete medium, and 10% dimethyl sulfoxide. CUT&Tag was performed by Active Motif as a service using an H3.3-validated antibody.
Proximity ligation assay
Cells were seeded at a density of 2.5 × 10
4
cells on fibronectin-coated 10 mm German Glass coverslips placed in 4-well plates and cultured for 24 h. The cells were washed once with PBS, fixed in methanol for 5 min at room temperature, and then blocked for an hour using Duolink Blocking Solution. All subsequent washes were 4 ml at room temperature, and the coverslips were transferred to 6-well plates. All reactions and incubations occurred on parafilm taped inside a humidity chamber. HDAC7 antibody was added at a 1:100 dilution into Duolink Antibody Diluent, 50 μl was placed on each coverslip, and incubated overnight at 4 °C. The coverslips were washed three times in 4 ml of 1× wash buffer A for 5 min each. The anti-rabbit PLUS probe was diluted 1:5 in the Duolink Antibody Diluent, and 40 μl was applied to each coverslip and incubated for 1 h at 37 °C. The coverslips were washed three times with 1× wash buffer A for 5 min. The conjugated H3.3-MINUS antibody (created with the Duolink Probemaker MINUS) was diluted at 1:300 in PLA probe diluent, and 50 μl was added to each coverslip and incubated overnight at 4 °C. The coverslips were washed three times with 1× wash buffer A for 5 min. The 5× Duolink ligation buffer was diluted 1:5 in high-purity water, and the ligase was added at a 1:40 dilution immediately before adding 40 μl of the mix to the coverslips. The cells were then incubated for 30 min at 37 °C. The coverslips were washed three times with 1× wash buffer A for 5 min. The 5× Duolink amplification buffer was diluted 1:5 in high-purity water, and the polymerase was added in a 1:80 dilution immediately before applying 40 μl of the amplification solution to the coverslips and incubated for 100 min at 37 °C. The amplification buffer was light sensitive and protected from light throughout as well as for all subsequent steps. The slides were washed two times in 1× wash buffer B for 10 min, then one time in 0.01× wash buffer B for 1 min. Two coverslips were mounted onto each slide using the Vectashield Mounting Medium with DAPI. They were left to dry for at least 1 h and imaged using the 83× objective on a Zeiss Axio Imager with the ApoTome 2.0. The slides were stored at −20 °C. Negative controls with either the conjugated H3.3-MINUS antibody or the HDAC7 antibody were excluded.
DNA fiber assay
GSCs were transfected with siControl or siHDAC7 as described above. DNA fiber assays were performed according to previously published protocols (
59
). Quantification of fibers from three images obtained from two independent experiments was performed using a semiautomated technique available in the DNA Stranding software package (
60

In each group, individual fibers were segmented automatically using the software’s prespecified input parameters, and the 20-min pulse labeling of chlorodeoxyuridine and iododeoxyuridine was selected according to the DNA fiber assay protocol. After automatic segmentation, a manual review of individual fiber labels was conducted to remove erroneously selected fiber segmentations and correct apparent mistakes, in line with previously published methods. A total of 291 fibers from cells transfected with siControl and 167 fibers from cells transfected with siHDAC7 were identified and quantified in the final analysis. Quantitative comparison of replication fork speed and chlorodeoxyuridine and iododeoxyuridine ratio metrics was performed using GraphPad Prism.
